record.context_brief: Problem 7: existence of positive integer solutions
record.original_question: Given a Diophantine equation, determine whether it has a solution in positive integers.

evidence.quote: One may also study the problem of solution existence in positive integers.
Problem 7. Given a Diophantine equation, determine whether it has a solution in positive integers.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Decide the following algorithmic problem: given as input a polynomial equation $P(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) = 0$ with integer coefficients in finitely many variables, determine whether there exist positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ such that $P(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) = 0$. Specifically, does there exist an algorithm that, on every such input, terminates and correctly outputs "yes" or "no" according to whether positive integer solutions exist?
artifact.status_search_result: This is the positive-integer variant of Hilbert's tenth problem. By the Matiyasevich–Robinson–Davis–Putnam (MRDP) theorem (1970), Hilbert's tenth problem over the nonnegative/positive integers is undecidable: there is no algorithm that decides solvability of an arbitrary Diophantine equation in positive integers. The variants over $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$, and $\mathbb{Z}$ are all equivalent and all undecidable.

status_evidence.title: Hilbert's tenth problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Matiyasevich's theorem, also called the MRDP theorem, implies that no such algorithm exists.
status_evidence.claim: Solvability of Diophantine equations in (positive) integers is algorithmically undecidable.
